title: Redwood POC Weekly Sync - Benchmark Review vs Baseline Provider
summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark results comparing Redwood Dedicated config vs baseline provider. Redwood showed lower p50 latency for most workloads and higher sustainable throughput with batching and KV cache enabled; baseline had better cold-start times on small bursts. Discussed tuning (batch size, quantization), network egress impact, and next steps: share full benchmark spreadsheet, run 24-hour sustained throughput test, schedule deep-dive on p99 tail latency and autoscaler settings, and provide dedicated pricing for pilot capacity.
action_items: Owner: Liam O'Connor (SE) - Provide per-model benchmark CSV and raw logs (latency histogram + QPS) - Due: 2025-12-19
Owner: Ben Thompson (Customer) - Share test harness config and request templates used against baseline - Due: 2025-12-19
Owner: Maya Chen (AE) - Send Redwood Dedicated pilot pricing and commitment options - Due: 2025-12-18
Owner: Sofia Ruiz (Customer) - Validate network peering perf numbers and share VPC egress estimates - Due: 2025-12-22
next_steps: Redwood to upload full benchmark spreadsheet to shared drive
Run a 24-hour sustained throughput run on both Redwood Dedicated and baseline next week
Schedule p99 tail latency deep-dive with infra team (SE-led)
Customer to confirm pilot size and initial start date for Dedicated trial
transcript:
Meeting Header: Date: 2025-12-17 Time: 10:00 UTC Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Jared Patel (Acme Head of ML), Sofia Ruiz (Acme Infra), Ben Thompson (Acme ML Eng)

00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, uh this is our weekly poc sync to go over the benchmark numbers you saw in the sheet. quick sanity check on attendees?
00:07 Jared Patel: yep that's right, we got the sheet, thanks. Sofia and Ben are with me.
00:11 Liam O'Connor: hi all, i'll be walking through the numbers from the run we did last thursday. small note - some of the models were run with int8 quant and some with fp16; that's marked but there's a couple of spots where the auto-labeling got a little off so i'll call that out.
00:25 Ben Thompson: cool, thanks liam. main things we care about are p50, p95, throughput at 100 rps and 500 rps, and also the cost delta vs our current baseline provider.
00:34 Maya Chen: perfect, we'll focus on that. quick headline: Redwood Dedicated with KV cache and adaptive batching hit p50 ~40ms on the small chat model, p95 ~220ms; baseline provider p50 was ~72ms, p95 ~300ms. for the larger generation model Redwood p50 ~180ms, p95 ~780ms; baseline p50 ~220ms, p95 ~950ms. throughput sustained at 500 qps with batching + cache was stable on our Dedicated config, baseline started to fall off around 420 qps.
01:02 Jared Patel: those numbers look promising — did you keep the same request patterns? our harness had a bit more variability, like some 1k token prompts.
01:08 Liam O'Connor: yes we matched the harness you sent but we also ran a second run with the long tail prompts (1k tokens). for long sequences the cost per token becomes more dominant and we saw the variance increase; Redwood still maintained lower average latency but p99 widened a bit during sustained long seqs.
01:26 Sofia Ruiz: can you explain the KV cache impact? i thought cache mostly helps chat style with prefix reuse. we have a lot of analytic calls that don't reuse tokens.
01:33 Liam O'Connor: correct — KV cache helps when there's prefix reuse, so chat is where you see 2-4x effective latency improvements for subsequent calls. for one-off analytic calls there's less benefit; we rely on batching optimizations and model kernel selection to push throughput there. in the mixed workload we saw a combined improvement of ~25% CPU/GPU time per token.
01:52 Ben Thompson: there's a line in the sheet where the baseline had a much faster cold-start for a new model instance, like sub-second warm-up. was that the baseline's autoscaler behavior?
01:59 Liam O'Connor: yes that's likely down to instance startup + cached model reservoirs on their infra. Redwood's Dedicated config we used was optimized for steady-state throughput; cold starts can be tuned by keeping a min pool or using warm instances. we didn't enable min-pool aggressively in that run to be fair to cost comparisons.
02:18 Jared Patel: what's the tail latency story — p99 or p99.9?
02:22 Liam O'Connor: in the baseline run p99 was around 1.6s for the larger model; in our Dedicated run p99 was ~1.1s. p99.9 is noisy on both, occasionally hitting 2.5-3s on the baseline during bursts, Redwood stayed under 2s most of the time. again those are with our current autoscaler defaults.
02:42 Sofia Ruiz: any network egress differences? we saw outbound egress costs spike in baseline because they ran in a different region, and cross-region calls added latency.
02:50 Maya Chen: good call — region placement matters. For the benchmark we kept both runs in the same region but baseline had some helper services in a different region which added 30-60ms occasionally. Redwood can run in your preferred cloud region or Dedicated in your VPC which removes that cross-region hop.
03:06 Ben Thompson: you mentioned quantization — int8 vs fp16. how stable are the quality results? we can't sacrifice more than 1-2% eval metric delta.
03:14 Liam O'Connor: during the runs we ran an eval set for quality; int8 introduced a small delta (~0.8% BLEU-like metric drop on the summary task), fp16 was largely indistinguishable. we can run a targeted eval and return the per-prompt delta to you.
03:28 Jared Patel: ok that's good. cost - what was the cost per 1M tokens comparison?
03:33 Maya Chen: rough ballpark from the pilot config: Redwood Dedicated pilot (amortized) was ~15% lower per-token vs baseline when using batching + KV cache; without batching the delta narrows. also remember baseline had additional network egress and some hidden replication costs. we'll send a detailed cost model.
03:50 Sofia Ruiz: in terms of security/compliance, did you capture audit logs and SSO integration in the pilot? our security team will ask.
03:57 Maya Chen: yes the Dedicated trial includes audit logs, SAML SSO and optional KMS integration if you want to manage keys. we also have SOC 2 docs and can share that — we'll include security pack in the next email.
04:10 Ben Thompson: one weird thing — in one run latency spiked for Redwood at t=03:12 in the logs, any idea?
04:16 Liam O'Connor: i saw that too, that's likely a kernel switch combined with a cache flush; there's a known case where the runtime will recompile a fused kernel on first use under certain sequence lengths. we can avoid that by pre-warming those code paths or pinning the kernel selection. action: i'll include the raw logs so you can see the flamegraph.
04:34 Jared Patel: are there limits on model variants? we might want to test a trimmed quantized variant plus a full fp16 fallback for critical queries.
04:41 Maya Chen: you can pin model versions and have automatic fallback to a higher-precision variant for the few queries that need it. the rollout controls let you run canaries and A/B tests.
04:49 Sofia Ruiz: great. next steps i want: the full CSV, the raw logs, and a list of config knobs you changed for the run. also pricing.
04:56 Maya Chen: confirmed — we'll send: 1) full benchmark spreadsheet + raw latency histograms 2) run configs (batch sizes, min pool, quant settings) 3) Dedicated pilot pricing and sizing options 4) security pack (SOC2 + KMS + SSO docs).
05:10 Ben Thompson: can we also schedule the p99 deep-dive the week after next? want to bring a couple infra folks.
05:15 Liam O'Connor: yes i'll lead that, let's lock a 60 minute slot and i'll prepare traces and kernel-level notes.
05:21 Maya Chen: perfect, we'll put calendar invites after this meeting. thanks everyone.
05:25 Jared Patel: thanks all, very helpful.

Meeting Recap: Redwood outperforms baseline on average latency and sustained throughput when batching and KV cache are used; baseline has slightly faster cold-starts in some cases. Primary follow-ups are raw logs, spreadsheet, pricing, and a p99 deep-dive.
notes: Transcript contains occasional transcription errors and swapped acronyms (e.g., K-V cache sometimes transcribed as KVchache). Some speaker labels generic at times but context preserved.
